hints: Look at the fuzzy edge facing the lumen in Fig. 5.1 and think about what very fine projections and surface coating the bronchus lining has in life.
walkthrough:
Picture the Living Lining**
The bronchus is lined by a ciliated epithelium with goblet cells. In life the surface facing the air is not smooth. It has hundreds of tiny cilia beating in a thin layer of mucus to move mucus up and out.

Why Good Resolution Still Looks Blurred**
Cilia are very small and closely packed, and mucus scatters light. Even with good resolution the light microscope cannot separate each fine cilium sharply, so the whole luminal border looks slightly fuzzy rather than a crisp line.
Final answer: The luminal surface bears cilia (ciliated epithelium), which are too fine to be sharply resolved and / or covered in mucus, so the edge appears blurred.

hints: Start from the idea that the bronchial epithelium is a mixture - not every columnar cell in Fig. 5.1 does the same job.
Think about how a stain works - cells with different chemicals inside and with denser contents like large nuclei will hold more stain and let less light through, so look darker.
walkthrough:
Two Jobs, Two Cell Types**
Side by side you have tall ciliated cells that sweep mucus, and paler goblet cells that secrete mucus. Cell D and cell L are different types, so their cytoplasm and contents are chemically different.

Why Stain Makes One Dark and One Light**
In a stained section, different chemicals take up stain differently. A cell with denser cytoplasm or with more of the nucleus in the section holds more stain. More stain means less light passes through to your eye, so it looks dark. A goblet cell full of unstained mucus vesicles lets more light through, so it looks light.

Final answer: The epithelium contains two cell types, ciliated epithelial cells and goblet cells; they stain differentially / have different densities, so denser cells with more stain absorb more light and appear darker (D) while less dense cells appear lighter (L).

hints: Compare the look of box A as a smooth continuous sheet with box B as isolated rounded spaces - what does that tell you about how the cells are packed?
Recall the typical cell shape for a contracting tissue versus a supporting tissue - spindle and tightly packed versus rounded and spaced out in gaps.
Now link structure to job - which tissue can shorten to narrow the tube, and which tissue is rigid to hold the tube open?
walkthrough:
Identify Tissue A From Its Look**
Box B is given as cartilage with its rounded cells sitting alone in little gaps called lacunae. Box A is a pale continuous band. That is smooth muscle made of smooth muscle cells, not chondrocytes.

Contrast the Cell Arrangement**
Smooth muscle cells are long, spindle-shaped and packed closely together so they can pull together. Cartilage cells are more rounded and isolated from each other in lacunae surrounded by matrix. Muscle has a blood supply, cartilage has no blood vessels and is surrounded by perichondrium.

Contrast the Jobs in the Bronchus**
Because of that structure, tissue A can contract and relax to alter the diameter of the airway lumen and control airflow. Tissue B cannot contract. It is firm and elastic to support the wall, preventing collapse and holding the bronchus open.

Final answer: Tissue A is smooth muscle, tissue B is cartilage. Structure: A has closely packed spindle-shaped / elongated muscle cells, B has rounded chondrocytes isolated in lacunae. Function: A is contractile and changes / controls airway diameter, B is non-contractile and supports / prevents collapse and keeps bronchus open.
